TwoComplement

@Metadata { @TechnologyRoot }

This library is intended to simplify using Swift to model signal processing blocks implemented using two's complement arithmetic. Think of it a start towards extending Swift to System-Swift, as an alternative to System-C. The library is a port from a Python library so much (but not all) of the debugging has been done.

TwoCmplt

The intended use of this library is that when developing a fixed-point hardware system, the system is first simulated at a high level, but bit-accurate, to do most of the debugging. The author usually does this using Python, but ideally, Swift will make the simulations much faster. Once the bit-accurate systems are debugged and characterized (note: we are still using Python's numpy and scipy's FFT's and matplotlib.pyplot for characterization, for now) at a high level, then they would be translated into either verilog for FPGA's or custom silicon or CUDA. The Swift realization would be used to help verify the hardware implementation. The fantasy is to eventually have genertors do the translations (aside: this could be an interesting Master's thesis topic?)

Most functions are methods in the TwoCmplt struct. Many signal processing systems, for example, fixed-point digital filters involve processing two's complement fixed-point integers of a specified bit length. This library makes public a large number of functions intended to be bit-accurate to hardware realizations of systems that use twos-complement operations. This library was implemented in Swift because a) it is relatively fast, and b) supports many types that make using the library much cleaner, such as operator over-loading. Swift is well suited for fast system level simulations of digital systems. This package is currently only supported in linux (but should port easily to macOS). The documentation and debugging are on-going. Doing the documentation using docc is perhaps a large mistake, but currently, it is too time-consuming to correct.

Summary

A TwoCmplt struct contains the value (called value, an Int) of the two's complement variable, and properties defining the variable. These properties describe the number of bits used for the variable (nbits, an Int), whether the variable is considered to be signed or unsigned (signed, a Bool), and the precision if it's not zero (prec, an Int). The precision determines how the value should be scaled when it is combined with other two's complement integers similar to how Matlab represents two's complement variables using it's "fi" types. (https://www.mathworks.com/help/fixedpoint/ug/perform-fixed-point-arithmetic.html)

Filters

There are a number of examples of simulating digital filters in the Examples module. Some of these use the Fixed Coefficient Multiplier, some assume a generic multiplier, and some are restricted to just using shifts. One of the examples show how a filter can be completely defined from a simple Yaml file; it's update order is determined using Kahn's Topological Sort algorithm.

CoeffMlt

This is one of the examples showing the use of the TwoCmplt library. When doing two's complement signal processing, the mulitplication operation is expensive in terms of hardware size and speed. In many two's complement signal processing systems, many if not most, multiplications are by fixed coefficients, that either never change, or only change slowly over many clock periods. This library introduces a new approach for realizing fixed point multiplications that is faster and requires less hardware. It is based on dividing the "signal" into nibbles of 4 bits each. Each nibble controls a 16 word to 1 word multiplexor. The inputs to the multipliers are multiples of the coefficient, or shifted right versions of multiples of the coefficients. The outputs of the multiplexors are added together, normally using carry-save adders (yet to be implemented - coming soon).
